course.title: UI and UX Design
course.tagline: Design apps and websites people enjoy using, from research and wireframes to polished Figma screens.

days.title: What UX and UI Mean
days.goal: Understand the difference between UX (how it works) and UI (how it looks).

video.title: Free Figma UX Design UI Essentials Course

steps: Write down one app you love and one app you find hard to use, and say why for each.
List three things that make an app easy: clear labels, obvious buttons, fast feedback.
Open a food delivery app and note the steps from opening it to ordering food.
Sketch the same flow on paper with boxes and arrows.
days.task: Pick an app you use daily and write down its three best and three worst moments.
days.challenge: Redesign one confusing screen of an app on paper in five minutes.

options: Designing how a product feels and works: easy, clear and useful
quiz.explain: UX is about the experience: can people do what they came to do, easily and without confusion?

options: Designing what people see and touch: screens, buttons, colours and type
quiz.explain: UI is the visible part: the layout, colours, type and buttons people see and tap.

quiz.q: Which comes first, UX or UI?
options: UX: you work out how it should work before you design how it looks
quiz.explain: First you design the flow and the structure (UX), then you design the look (UI).

days.title: Getting Started with Figma
days.goal: Set up Figma and learn its basic tools.

video.title: Learn Figma for UI/UX Design

steps: Create a free Figma account at figma.com.
Make a new design file and a frame the size of a phone screen.
Draw a rectangle, a circle and a line with the shape tools.
Add a text layer, change its size and colour, and move it with the arrow keys.
days.task: Make a simple welcome screen in Figma with a heading, a short line of text and a button.
days.challenge: Draw five different shapes and change the colour of each one.

options: A free design tool in the browser for drawing screens, wireframes and prototypes
quiz.explain: Figma is where designers draw app and website screens, make prototypes and work together.

quiz.q: What is a frame in Figma?
options: A canvas shaped like a screen or a page that holds your design
quiz.explain: A frame is the artboard: a phone screen, a desktop page or a card that your design sits on.

options: The stacked pieces of your design: shapes, text and images, one on top of another
quiz.explain: Every shape, text and image is a layer. Layers stack, and you can select, move and rename each one.

days.title: Design Thinking: Empathise
days.goal: Start with the user: learn who they are and what they need.

video.title: Free Figma UX Design UI Essentials Course

steps: Pick a problem to solve, like helping students find cheap food near campus.
Write down who the users are and what they are trying to do.
List five questions you would ask a real user about this problem.
Ask one real person two of your questions and write down their answers.
days.task: Interview one person about an app they use and write down three frustrations they mention.
days.challenge: Write a one-sentence problem statement for your chosen problem.

quiz.q: What is the first step of design thinking?
options: Empathise: understand the users and their problem
quiz.explain: Design thinking starts with empathy: understanding real users before you draw anything.

options: One clear sentence that says who has the problem, what it is and why it matters
quiz.explain: A problem statement focuses the work: who, what problem, and why it matters.

options: Because your guesses about users are often wrong
quiz.explain: Guessing about users is risky. Talking to them shows you what they really need.

days.title: User Research on a Zero Budget
days.goal: Learn simple research methods that cost nothing.

video.title: UI / UX Design Tutorial – From Zero to Hero with Wireframe + Prototype + Design in Figma

steps: Write five interview questions about your problem, open-ended not yes/no.
Interview two people and write down what they say in their own words.
Watch one person use a similar app and note where they pause or get stuck.
Sort your notes into groups: needs, frustrations and wishes.
days.task: Interview two people about how they order food and write a short summary of what you learned.
days.challenge: Watch a friend use an app for two minutes and note every moment of confusion.

options: A question that lets people answer in their own words, like 'Tell me about the last time you...'
quiz.explain: Open questions get stories. Yes/no questions get one-word answers that teach you little.

quiz.q: Why watch people use an app instead of only asking them?
options: Because people often do things differently from what they say they do
quiz.explain: Watching shows real behaviour: pauses, wrong taps and workarounds that people forget to mention.

quiz.q: What do you do with research notes?
options: Group them into themes so patterns appear
quiz.explain: Grouping notes into themes reveals patterns: the same need or frustration mentioned by several people.

days.title: Personas
days.goal: Turn research into a persona: a clear picture of one typical user.

video.title: Figma Tutorial for Beginners - Complete Course 2025

steps: Pick the most common user from your research notes.
Give them a name, age, job and a photo (use a placeholder image).
Write their goals: what are they trying to achieve?
Write their frustrations: what gets in their way?
days.task: Make a one-page persona for your food app with a name, goals and frustrations.
days.challenge: Write a quote in the persona's own words about their main frustration.

options: A made-up character built from research that stands for a group of real users
quiz.explain: A persona is a realistic character based on research. It keeps the team focused on real users.

quiz.q: Why give a persona a name and a photo?
options: So the team talks about a real-feeling person instead of 'the user'
quiz.explain: A name and face make the persona feel real, so decisions get made for a person, not an abstract idea.

options: Goals, frustrations, needs and a quote, all based on research
quiz.explain: A persona holds what matters for design: what they want, what blocks them, and how they talk about it.

days.title: User Journey Mapping
days.goal: Map the steps a user takes and find the painful moments.

video.title: How To Create UX Personas

steps: List the steps your persona takes from realising a need to finishing the task.
For each step, note what they do, think and feel.
Mark the moments where they feel frustrated or confused.
Circle the one moment that matters most to fix.
days.task: Draw a journey map for ordering food: from hungry to food delivered, with feelings at each step.
days.challenge: Find the worst moment in the journey and write one idea to fix it.

quiz.q: What is a user journey map?
options: A drawing of the steps a user takes, with what they do, think and feel at each step
quiz.explain: A journey map shows the whole experience as a timeline, including feelings, so you can see where it breaks.

quiz.q: Why note feelings on a journey map?
options: Because the worst feelings show you exactly where to improve
quiz.explain: Feelings reveal pain points. A step that makes users anxious or angry is a step to fix.

options: A moment in the journey where the user struggles, waits or gets confused
quiz.explain: A pain point is a moment of friction. Finding them is the point of the map.

days.title: Project 1: Research and Persona Pack
days.goal: Do real research and turn it into a persona and a journey map.

video.title: How to Use Journey Mapping to Improve Your Online Sales | The Journey

steps: Interview at least three people about your chosen problem.
Write a one-page summary of what you learned.
Build a persona from the research with goals, frustrations and a quote.
Draw a journey map and mark the top three pain points.
days.task: Finish the research pack: summary, persona and journey map.
days.challenge: Share your persona with one person and ask if it feels like a real person.

options: What real users need, in their own words, with evidence
quiz.explain: Good research gives evidence: quotes and patterns from real users, not your opinions.

quiz.q: How many people should you interview for a small project?
options: Three to five is enough to see patterns
quiz.explain: Three to five interviews usually reveal the main patterns. More helps, but small projects start here.

options: Details that come from real research, not invention
quiz.explain: A persona is believable when every detail traces back to something a real user said or did.

project.title: Research and Persona Pack
project.brief: Interview at least three people about a real problem, write a summary of what you learned, build a persona from the research, and draw a journey map with the top three pain points marked.
checks: At least three people were interviewed.
A one-page summary of the research exists.
A persona exists with goals, frustrations and a quote.
A journey map shows the steps with feelings.
The top three pain points are marked on the map.
Every persona detail traces back to the research.

days.title: Information Architecture
days.goal: Organise content so people can find what they need.

video.title: Journey Mapping in UX Design

steps: List all the screens your app will need.
Group them into sections, like Home, Search, Orders and Profile.
Draw a site map: boxes for screens, lines for how they connect.
Check that any screen is reachable in three taps or fewer.
days.task: Draw a site map for your food app with every screen and how they connect.
days.challenge: Ask a friend to find 'my past orders' on your site map and time them.

options: How content and screens are organised so people can find things
quiz.explain: Information architecture is the organisation of an app: what goes where, and how screens connect.

options: A diagram of all the screens and how they link together
quiz.explain: A site map shows every screen as a box and the links between them, so you can see the whole structure.

quiz.q: Why keep things three taps away?
options: It is a rule of law
Because people give up when they have to dig deep to find something
quiz.explain: The deeper something is buried, the fewer people find it. Keep important things close to the surface.

days.title: Wireframes
days.goal: Sketch the structure of screens before you design how they look.

video.title: UI/UX Design Full Course 2026

steps: Sketch your home screen on paper with boxes for images and lines for text.
Sketch three more screens: search results, item detail and checkout.
Use simple grey boxes: no colours, no real images, no fancy fonts.
Show your sketches to one person and ask them what each screen is for.
days.task: Sketch wireframes for all the main screens of your app on paper.
days.challenge: Redraw the one screen your tester misunderstood.

options: A simple sketch of a screen's layout: where things go, without colours or detail
quiz.explain: A wireframe is a skeleton. It shows the layout and structure so you can test the flow before you polish the look.

quiz.q: Why use grey boxes instead of real content?
options: So you focus on layout and flow, not on colours and pictures
quiz.explain: Grey boxes keep the focus on structure. Real content distracts from whether the layout works.

options: To catch layout and flow problems while they are cheap to fix
quiz.explain: A paper sketch is cheap to change. Finding a problem now saves hours of redesign later.

days.title: Wireframes in Figma
days.goal: Turn paper sketches into clean digital wireframes in Figma.

video.title: Zero-Budget User Research: 4 Methods for Beginners

steps: Recreate your paper wireframes as frames in Figma.
Use rectangles for images and lines for text.
Keep everything grey and use the same spacing everywhere.
Link the frames together so you can click through the flow.
days.task: Build digital wireframes for all your app's screens in Figma.
days.challenge: Click through the flow and check every screen connects to the next.

options: So you can share them, link them into a flow and change them easily
quiz.explain: Digital wireframes are easy to share, link into a clickable flow and update when feedback comes in.

options: A simple wireframe with boxes and lines, focused on layout not looks
quiz.explain: Low-fidelity means rough and simple. It is for testing structure, not for showing the final look.

quiz.q: How do you link wireframes in Figma?
options: With the prototyping tab: drag from one frame to the next
quiz.explain: Figma's prototyping lets you link frames, so clicking a button in one frame opens the next.

days.title: Usability Testing
days.goal: Test your wireframes with real people and learn from what happens.

video.title: Guide to prototyping in Figma

steps: Write three tasks for a tester, like 'Order a burger for delivery'.
Ask a tester to do the tasks while thinking out loud.
Watch and write down where they pause, tap wrong or ask questions.
Do not help them: watch what they do on their own.
days.task: Test your wireframes with two people and write down the top five problems.
days.challenge: Fix the worst problem and test again with one person.

options: Asking people if they like the design
Watching real people try real tasks and noting where they struggle
quiz.explain: Usability testing watches people do tasks. Where they struggle shows you what to fix.

quiz.q: Why ask testers to think out loud?
options: So you hear what they expect and where they get confused
quiz.explain: Thinking aloud reveals what the tester expects and where the design breaks that expectation.

options: Because helping hides the problems you need to find
quiz.explain: If you help, you will never see the struggle. The struggle is the data.

days.title: Colour and Typography
days.goal: Choose colours and fonts that are clear, readable and on-brand.

video.title: Figma Prototyping Transitions Tutorial

steps: Pick three colours for your app: a main colour, a second colour and a neutral.
Check the contrast between text and background is strong enough to read.
Pick one font for headings and one for body text.
Set text sizes: big for headings, medium for body, small for captions.
days.task: Build a colour and type style guide for your app in Figma.
days.challenge: Test your colours on a phone screen in sunlight: can you still read them?

quiz.q: Why limit yourself to three colours?
options: It is a rule of law
So the app looks calm and consistent instead of messy
quiz.explain: A small palette keeps the design consistent. Too many colours make an app look noisy and random.

options: The difference in brightness between text and its background
quiz.explain: Contrast is how much text stands out from its background. Low contrast text is hard to read.

quiz.q: Why use two fonts at most?
options: So the design feels consistent and the fonts do not fight each other
quiz.explain: One font for headings and one for body text gives variety without chaos.

days.title: Visual Design Principles
days.goal: Use spacing, alignment and hierarchy to make screens look clean.

video.title: Free Figma UX Design UI Essentials Course

steps: Use the same spacing between elements everywhere on a screen.
Align everything to a grid: left edges line up.
Make the most important thing biggest and boldest.
Use white space to separate groups of related items.
days.task: Redesign one of your wireframes with proper spacing, alignment and hierarchy.
days.challenge: Compare your old and new versions and note three improvements.

options: Arranging elements so the eye sees the most important thing first
quiz.explain: Hierarchy uses size, weight and position to guide the eye to what matters most first.

options: Because lined-up edges make a design feel calm and professional
quiz.explain: Aligned elements feel organised. Random edges feel messy, even if people cannot say why.

options: The space between elements that separates groups and lets the design breathe
quiz.explain: White space is not wasted space. It separates groups and makes screens easier to scan.

days.title: Project 2: Wireframes and Test Results
days.goal: Turn your research into wireframes and test them with real people.

video.title: Learn Figma for UI/UX Design

steps: Build digital wireframes in Figma for all your app's main screens.
Link them into a clickable flow.
Test the flow with three people using real tasks.
Write a short report: the five biggest problems and how you fixed them.
days.task: Finish the wireframes, the flow and the test report.
days.challenge: Fix the top three problems found in testing.

quiz.q: What should a test report include?
options: The tasks, what happened, the problems found and the fixes
quiz.explain: A test report records what testers did, where they struggled, and what you changed because of it.

quiz.q: How many testers do you need for wireframes?
options: Three to five usually finds the main problems
quiz.explain: Three to five testers find most big problems. More testers find the same problems again.

quiz.q: What do you do with a problem you cannot fix yet?
options: Write it down and note it for the next round
quiz.explain: Write it down. A known problem you plan to fix is better than a forgotten one.

project.title: Wireframes and Test Results
project.brief: Build digital wireframes in Figma for all your app's main screens, link them into a clickable flow, test the flow with three people using real tasks, and write a short report with the five biggest problems and your fixes.
checks: Digital wireframes exist for all main screens.
The wireframes link into a clickable flow.
Three people tested the flow with real tasks.
A report lists the five biggest problems.
The top three problems are fixed.
The report explains what changed and why.

days.title: High-Fidelity Design in Figma
days.goal: Turn wireframes into polished screens with real colours, images and text.

video.title: Free Figma UX Design UI Essentials Course

steps: Replace grey boxes with real images and real text.
Apply your colour palette and fonts to every screen.
Use components for repeated parts like buttons and cards.
Check spacing and alignment on every screen.
days.task: Turn your home screen wireframe into a polished high-fidelity design.
days.challenge: Make a component for your main button and reuse it on three screens.

options: A polished design that looks like the real app, with real colours, images and text
quiz.explain: High-fidelity means it looks like the finished product. It is what you show to stakeholders and developers.

quiz.q: What is a component in Figma?
options: A reusable design piece, like a button, that you can use on many screens and update in one place
quiz.explain: Components are reusable pieces. Change the master component and every copy updates.

options: So repeated parts stay identical and you can change them all at once
quiz.explain: Components keep buttons, cards and headers consistent across every screen.

days.title: Design Systems and Components
days.goal: Build a small design system: buttons, inputs, cards and colours in one place.

video.title: UI / UX Design Tutorial – From Zero to Hero with Wireframe + Prototype + Design in Figma

steps: Make a Figma page called 'Design System'.
Add your colours as styles and your fonts as text styles.
Build components for a button, an input field and a card.
Use only these components on your screens.
days.task: Build a design system page with colours, text styles and three components.
days.challenge: Redesign one screen using only your design system components.

options: A shared set of colours, fonts and components that keeps a product consistent
quiz.explain: A design system is the single source of truth for how a product looks and behaves.

options: Saved colours and text settings you can apply anywhere and update in one place
quiz.explain: Styles save a colour or text setting. Change the style once and every use updates.

quiz.q: Why does a design system save time?
options: Because you reuse pieces instead of redrawing them on every screen
quiz.explain: Reuse beats redrawing. A design system means you build once and use everywhere.

days.title: Prototyping in Figma
days.goal: Make your designs clickable so people can feel the real flow.

video.title: Figma Tutorial for Beginners - Complete Course 2025

steps: Link your screens with the prototyping tab.
Set the transition for each link, like a slide or a fade.
Add a tap interaction to your main button.
Play the prototype and click through the whole flow.
days.task: Build a clickable prototype of your app with at least five screens.
days.challenge: Share the prototype link with one person and ask them to try it.

options: A clickable model of your design that feels like the real app
quiz.explain: A prototype links your screens so people can tap through the flow like a real app, without any code.

options: The animation between two screens, like a slide or a fade
quiz.explain: Transitions animate the move from one screen to the next, which makes the prototype feel real.

options: To test the flow and catch problems before developers build it
quiz.explain: A prototype lets you test the experience cheaply. Fixing a prototype is fast; fixing a built app is slow.

days.title: Micro-interactions and Animation
days.goal: Add small animations that make the app feel alive.

video.title: How To Create UX Personas

steps: Add a button that changes colour when pressed.
Animate a card that grows slightly when tapped.
Add a loading spinner for a screen that waits for data.
Keep animations short: under half a second.
days.task: Add three micro-interactions to your prototype: a button press, a card tap and a loading state.
days.challenge: Ask one person if the animations help or distract them.

options: A small animation that responds to one action, like a button press or a like
quiz.explain: Micro-interactions are tiny animations that confirm an action happened, like a heart filling when you tap like.

options: Because long animations feel slow and annoy users
quiz.explain: Animations under half a second feel instant. Longer ones feel like waiting.

options: That something happened and what changed
quiz.explain: Good animation shows cause and effect: you tapped, and this is what changed.

days.title: Accessibility in Design
days.goal: Design so everyone can use your app, including people with disabilities.

video.title: Learn Accessibility - Full a11y Tutorial

steps: Check that all text has strong contrast against its background.
Make touch targets at least 44 pixels so they are easy to tap.
Do not use colour alone to show meaning: add text or an icon too.
Test your screens in greyscale to check they still make sense.
days.task: Fix the accessibility issues in your designs: contrast, touch targets and colour-only meaning.
days.challenge: Check your app with a screen reader in mind: does every image have a label?

options: Designing so people with disabilities can use the product too
quiz.explain: Accessibility means people using screen readers, keyboards or other tools can still use your app fully.

quiz.q: Why not use colour alone to show meaning?
options: Because colour-blind users cannot tell red from green, so they miss the meaning
quiz.explain: Colour alone fails for colour-blind users. Add text or an icon so the meaning is clear to everyone.

options: The area you tap to activate something. It should be big enough to hit easily
quiz.explain: Touch targets should be at least 44 pixels, so fingers of all sizes can tap them without missing.

days.title: Design Handoff to Developers
days.goal: Prepare your designs so developers can build them exactly.

video.title: Journey Mapping in UX Design

steps: Name every layer clearly in Figma.
Add notes on spacing, colours and behaviour for each screen.
Export the images and icons developers will need.
Share the Figma file with a developer and walk them through it.
days.task: Prepare your app file for handoff: named layers, notes and exported assets.
days.challenge: Ask a developer (or a friend) if they can build one screen from your file alone.

options: Sharing your finished designs with developers, with the details they need to build them
quiz.explain: Handoff is when you give developers your designs plus specs: sizes, colours, spacing and behaviour.

options: So developers can find things and understand what each piece is
quiz.explain: Clear layer names like 'primary-button' tell developers what a piece is, instead of 'Rectangle 47'.

options: Spacing, colours, fonts, behaviour and what happens on tap or error
quiz.explain: Handoff notes answer the questions developers will ask: sizes, colours, and what happens in each state.

days.title: Project 3: Polished App Design and Prototype
days.goal: Turn your wireframes into a polished, clickable app design.

video.title: UI/UX Design Full Course 2026

steps: Design high-fidelity screens for all your app's main flows.
Build a design system with colours, text styles and components.
Link the screens into a clickable prototype.
Test the prototype with three people and fix the top problems.
days.task: Finish the polished design and prototype, and test it with three people.
days.challenge: Fix the top three problems found in testing.

options: Consistent colours, fonts, spacing and components on every screen
quiz.explain: Polish comes from consistency: the same colours, fonts and spacing everywhere.

quiz.q: Why test the polished prototype again?
options: Because new problems appear when the design is real and detailed
quiz.explain: Polished screens reveal new issues: text that is too small, images that distract, or flows that feel long.

quiz.q: What should you do with test feedback?
options: Fix the biggest problems first, then retest
quiz.explain: Fix the biggest problems first. Small polish can wait until the big issues are solved.

project.title: Polished App Design and Prototype
project.brief: Turn your wireframes into high-fidelity screens with a design system, link them into a clickable prototype, test it with three people, and fix the top problems.
checks: High-fidelity screens exist for all main flows.
A design system page has colours, text styles and components.
The screens link into a clickable prototype.
Three people tested the prototype.
The top three problems found are fixed.
The design is consistent across every screen.

days.title: Portfolio and Case Study
days.goal: Turn your project into a case study that shows how you think.

video.title: Zero-Budget User Research: 4 Methods for Beginners

steps: Write the story: the problem, your research, your design and the results.
Show your persona, journey map and wireframes.
Show before and after screens with the test findings.
End with what you learned and what you would do next.
days.task: Write a one-page case study of your app project.
days.challenge: Share it with one person and ask if they understand your process.

quiz.q: What is a design case study?
options: A story of a project: the problem, the process, the design and what you learned
quiz.explain: A case study shows how you think, not just what you made. Employers read it to see your process.

quiz.q: What should a case study show?
options: Research, wireframes, tests and final screens, with reasons for each decision
quiz.explain: A case study shows the journey: research, ideas, tests and results, with the reasons behind each choice.

options: Because it shows growth and honesty, which employers value
quiz.explain: Saying what you learned and what you would do next shows you can reflect and improve.

days.title: Design Critique and Feedback
days.goal: Give and receive design feedback that makes the work better.

video.title: Guide to prototyping in Figma

steps: Share your design with two people and ask for specific feedback.
Ask 'What is confusing?' instead of 'Do you like it?'.
Write down every piece of feedback before replying to any of it.
Pick the feedback that matches your research and act on it.
days.task: Get feedback on your app design from two people and fix the top three issues.
days.challenge: Give feedback on someone else's design using the same questions.

options: A structured look at a design to find what works and what to improve
quiz.explain: A critique examines a design against its goals and gives specific, useful feedback.

quiz.q: Why ask 'What is confusing?' instead of 'Do you like it?'?
options: Because 'like' gives no useful detail, while confusion points at real problems
quiz.explain: 'Do you like it' gets opinions. 'What is confusing' gets problems you can fix.

quiz.q: What should you do with feedback you disagree with?
options: Ask why, check it against your research, then decide
quiz.explain: Feedback you disagree with may still hold a truth. Check it against your research before you dismiss it.

days.title: Presenting Your Design
days.goal: Present your work clearly to people who are not designers.

video.title: Figma Prototyping Transitions Tutorial

steps: Write a five-minute talk: the problem, the users, your design and the results.
Pick your three best screens and explain each in one sentence.
Practise the talk out loud twice.
Prepare for two questions people might ask and write your answers.
days.task: Write and practise a five-minute presentation of your app design.
days.challenge: Present it to one person and note their questions.

quiz.q: What should a design presentation include?
options: The problem, the users, the design, the test results and what you learned
quiz.explain: A good presentation tells the story: the problem, who it is for, what you made, and whether it worked.

options: Because explaining simply proves you understand it and reveals gaps
quiz.explain: Presenting tests your understanding. If you cannot explain a decision simply, you do not fully understand it yet.

quiz.q: How should you handle a question you cannot answer?
options: Say you do not know and offer to check
quiz.explain: Saying 'I don't know, I'll check' is honest and builds trust. Guessing destroys it.

days.title: Designing for Mobile vs Desktop
days.goal: Design for small phone screens and big desktop screens, not just one.

video.title: Free Figma UX Design UI Essentials Course

steps: Take your app's home screen and sketch it for a phone and for a desktop.
On mobile, stack things vertically and make buttons thumb-friendly.
On desktop, use the wider space for side-by-side content.
Check that nothing important is hidden on the smaller screen.
days.task: Make a desktop version of your app's home screen in Figma.
days.challenge: List three things that change between your mobile and desktop layouts.

quiz.q: Why design for both mobile and desktop?
options: Because people use both, and each screen size needs its own layout
quiz.explain: A phone layout on a desktop wastes space. A desktop layout on a phone is unreadable. Each needs its own design.

quiz.q: What changes most on a small screen?
options: The layout: things stack vertically and menus hide behind a button
quiz.explain: Small screens stack content in one column and hide navigation behind a menu button.

options: A design that adapts its layout to the screen size
quiz.explain: Responsive design rearranges the same content to fit any screen, from phone to desktop.

days.title: Content Design: Writing for Screens
days.goal: Write clear words for buttons, labels and messages.

video.title: Learn Figma for UI/UX Design

steps: Rewrite three button labels so they say exactly what happens, like 'Place order'.
Write an error message that says what went wrong and what to do next.
Cut a long paragraph on one screen down to two short sentences.
Use plain words: 'buy' instead of 'purchase', 'help' instead of 'assistance'.
days.task: Rewrite all the text on your app's checkout screen in plain, short words.
days.challenge: Write an empty-state message for when a user has no orders yet.

options: Because the label tells the user exactly what will happen when they tap
quiz.explain: A clear label like 'Place order' sets the right expectation. A vague label like 'Submit' does not.

quiz.q: What makes a good error message?
options: It says what went wrong in plain words and what to do next
quiz.explain: A good error message explains the problem and the fix, so the user can carry on.

options: Because users scan fast and plain words are understood instantly
quiz.explain: Plain words are read and understood in seconds. Fancy words slow people down and cause mistakes.

days.title: Designing Empty States and Errors
days.goal: Design the screens people see when there is nothing to show or something goes wrong.

video.title: Free Figma UX Design UI Essentials Course

steps: Design an empty state for a list with no items: a friendly message and a button to add one.
Design an error screen for when the internet is off.
Design a loading state with a spinner and a short message.
Check that every screen in your app has a plan for empty, error and loading.
days.task: Design empty, error and loading states for your app's main list screen.
days.challenge: Write the words for each state in plain, friendly language.

options: A screen that shows when there is nothing to display yet, with a message and a next step
quiz.explain: An empty state appears when a list is empty. It should explain why and show what to do next.

options: Because errors happen, and a good error screen helps users recover instead of giving up
quiz.explain: Errors are part of the experience. A clear error screen with a fix keeps users from leaving.

quiz.q: What should a loading state show?
options: That something is happening and roughly how long it will take
quiz.explain: A loading state reassures users that the app is working, so they wait instead of tapping again.

days.title: Motion and Transitions in Prototypes
days.goal: Use movement in your prototype to show how screens connect.

video.title: UI / UX Design Tutorial – From Zero to Hero with Wireframe + Prototype + Design in Figma

steps: Add a slide transition when moving to the next screen.
Add a fade for a pop-up or a dialog.
Use Smart Animate in Figma to move an element smoothly between two frames.
Keep every transition under half a second.
days.task: Add Smart Animate to one flow in your prototype so a card grows into its detail screen.
days.challenge: Ask one person if the movement helps them follow the flow.

options: A Figma feature that animates matching elements between two frames
quiz.explain: Smart Animate finds the same element on two frames and moves it smoothly between them.

options: To show users where things came from and where they went
quiz.explain: Movement shows the relationship between screens: this card became this detail page.

options: When it is slow, distracting or happens on every single tap
quiz.explain: Animation should guide, not distract. If users notice the animation more than the content, it is too much.

days.title: Usability Heuristics: 10 Rules to Check Your Design
days.goal: Check your design against ten proven usability rules.

video.title: Figma Tutorial for Beginners - Complete Course 2025

steps: Read the ten usability heuristics by Jakob Nielsen.
Check your app against each one and write down where it breaks a rule.
Fix the two worst breaks you found.
Use the heuristics as a checklist for every new screen you design.
days.task: Run a heuristics check on your app and write down the three biggest issues.
days.challenge: Fix the biggest issue and note how the screen improved.

options: Ten general rules for good design, like 'show system status' and 'prevent errors'
quiz.explain: Heuristics are proven rules of thumb. Checking your design against them catches common problems.

quiz.q: What does 'visibility of system status' mean?
options: The app always shows what it is doing, like a loading spinner or a success message
quiz.explain: Users should always know what is happening. A spinner, a progress bar or a confirmation tells them.

options: Designing so mistakes are hard to make, like confirming before deleting
quiz.explain: The best error message is one the user never sees. Good design prevents the mistake in the first place.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your Design Project
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone project and plan your demo.

video.title: How To Create UX Personas

steps: List the projects you did and pick the strongest one to finish.
Write a short plan: the problem, the users, the screens and the prototype.
Practise explaining your design in simple words, as if to a friend.
Record a short video or write a short post showing your prototype.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your design.
days.challenge: Show your prototype to one person and note their questions, then improve it.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone design?
options: A real problem, real research, a tested prototype and a clear case study
quiz.explain: A good capstone solves a real problem with research, a tested prototype and a story that shows your thinking.

options: Because explaining simply proves you truly understand it
quiz.explain: If you can explain your design in simple words, you really understand it. That is what employers look for.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The problem, the users, the screens, the prototype and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the problem, the users, the screens and prototype, and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Design a Complete App: Research to Prototype
capstone.brief: Pick a real problem and design a complete app for it: research real users, build a persona and journey map, wireframe and test the flow, then design polished screens with a design system and a clickable prototype. Present it as a case study with a live prototype link.
checks: The design solves a real problem and you can explain the problem in one sentence.
At least three real users were interviewed and the research is documented.
A persona and journey map are based on the research.
Wireframes were tested with real people and the results are documented.
High-fidelity screens use a consistent design system.
A clickable prototype covers the main flows.
You can present the case study in under five minutes in simple words.
deliverables: A research pack: interview notes, persona and journey map.
High-fidelity screens and a design system in Figma.
A one-page case study of the project.
